title: Reverse Bits
statement:
A network driver reads 32-bit status words from a device that sends its bits in the opposite order: the device's bit 0 is your bit 31, its bit 1 is your bit 30, and so on.

Write def solution(n). n is an unsigned 32-bit integer (0 to 2^32 - 1). Treat it as exactly 32 bits, with leading zeros. Return the unsigned integer you get by reversing the order of those 32 bits. For example 1 is 000...001, which reversed is 100...000 = 2,147,483,648.

examples.why: 31 zeros and a 1, reversed: a 1 and 31 zeros, which is 2^31.

constraints: the result is also in that range

think.q: Why do the leading zeros matter?
think.a: The reversal is over exactly 32 positions. bin(1) is just '0b1', but as a 32-bit word it is 31 zeros and a 1. Reversed, that 1 moves to bit 31, giving 2^31. If you reversed only the visible digits, 1 would stay 1. Python ints have no fixed width, so you must count 32 positions yourself.

Take bits from the right of the input and push them onto the right of the output. Input 1011: take 1, output 1. Take 1, output 11. Take 0, output 110. Take 1, output 1101 = 13. Each step: out = (out << 1) | (n & 1), then n >>= 1.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Format as a 32-character binary string with format(n, '032b'), reverse it with [::-1], and parse it back with int(s, 2). It is short and correct. Interviewers usually then ask for the bit-operation version, which is what C, Java or hardware code would use.

Bit tricks: shift and mask. n & 1 reads the lowest bit, n >> 1 drops it, out << 1 makes room, and | bit writes it. Do it exactly 32 times. If the function runs millions of times, a follow-up is to precompute a 256-entry table of reversed bytes and combine 4 lookups.

1. out = 0.
  2. Repeat 32 times: out = (out << 1) | (n & 1); n >>= 1.
  3. Return out.
Looping a fixed 32 times, not 'while n', is what keeps the trailing zeros of the result.

0 (stays 0). 1 (becomes 2^31). 2^31 (becomes 1). All ones, 2^32 - 1 (stays the same). Palindromes like 0x80000001. Stopping the loop when n becomes 0, which drops the shifts for leading zeros and gives a too-small answer.

hints: Reverse a 4-bit number by hand first: read bits from the right end of the input and write them onto the right end of the output.
n & 1 is the lowest bit; n >> 1 removes it; (out << 1) | bit appends a bit to out.
Loop exactly 32 times, even after n becomes 0. Each extra shift places a zero, which is how the leading zeros of the input become trailing zeros of the output.
solution:
def solution(n):
    out = 0
    for _ in range(32):              # exactly 32 positions, leading zeros included
        out = (out << 1) | (n & 1)    # append n's lowest bit to out
        n >>= 1                       # move to n's next bit
    return out
explain:
Example 1, n = 43261596, which is 00000010100101000001111010011100 in 32 bits:

  • The loop reads bits from the right: 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, ... and appends each to out.
  • After 32 steps out holds the same bits in the opposite order: 00111001011110000010100101000000.

That is 964176192. The loop always runs 32 times: the input's 6 leading zeros turn into the output's 6 trailing zeros only because the last 6 shifts still happen after n has become 0. The work is constant: 32 steps for any input.

tests.label: low half
tests.why: the low 16 ones move to the high half

tests.why: a mixed pattern, every nibble different
